New Orleans is the parish, and it sits below the water

The city of New Orleans and Orleans Parish share the same boundaries, so one set of offices serves every address. The ground is what sets a house here apart. The city's average elevation is between 1 and 2 feet below sea level. Parts of Uptown reach about 20 feet at the base of the river levee, while the far reaches of Eastern New Orleans sit as low as 7 feet below sea level. Levees and drainage pumps hold the water back.

Hurricane Katrina in August 2005 flooded more than 80 percent of the city. Buyers and insurers remember that, so your address, lot elevation and flood history come up early in any talk about price and timing. The city's population estimate for July 1, 2025 is 362,154.

Recording fees and clerk rules

Six things tend to decide how smoothly a New Orleans sale goes: street elevation, the condition of the roof and foundation, open code cases, recorded liens, rental history and the tax bill. The paperwork side comes down to these numbers.

How a sale gets recorded in Orleans Parish

Every sale of New Orleans real estate is recorded with the Clerk of Civil District Court in its Land Records Division. State law makes that office responsible for preserving the parish property records forever and keeping them open to the public.

The old separate filing fees for mortgages, conveyances and notarial archives have been folded into a single recording fee. Checks are made payable to the Clerk of Court. In practice your notary or title company carries the signed act of sale to the clerk and pays from closing funds, but you should know where it goes and what it costs.

The documentary transaction tax

This is a city tax collected by the Notarial Archives on documents that transfer real estate. It applies to sales, donations, transfers, mortgages and commercial leases, and the seller is one of the parties responsible for paying it.

The tax is a flat $325 for most of these documents, due at recording. If it is not paid then, a billing form has to be filled out and the tax paid within 30 days, or interest and a $500 penalty are added. A single family residence or residential double whose document runs past 25 pages still pays $325, as long as a notarized statement confirms it is an owner-occupied single family residence or residential double.

A flat amount is easy to budget. Sellers get caught on the deadline, so settle in writing at the closing table who is paying it.

What happens when a house has code enforcement problems?

Open code cases and recorded liens follow the property, not the owner, so they have to be dealt with before or at a sale. The Department of Code Enforcement works through a set order of steps. It helps to know them if you inherited a house or lived elsewhere while it sat vacant.

  • Neighbors or inspectors report the property, and a case opens in the city's LAMA system. The target time from complaint to inspection is 30 days.
  • The Hearings Bureau researches title to find every owner and legal interest, then mails and posts a Notice of Noncompliance with a deadline to fix the violations.
  • If the violations are still open, a hearing is set 30 to 45 days after the compliance period. Owners must appear or send a representative, and hearing costs can be charged even when the work was finished before the date.
  • If the owner is found guilty and does not appeal, fix the problem or pay, a Notice of Judgment is filed with the recorder of mortgages 30 days after the hearing. That filing is a lien and lets the city clean up the property or seize it for sheriff's sale.

The city can cut lots, send a property to sheriff's sale or demolish a building. Sale proceeds first cover liens, taxes and sale costs, and any remainder goes to the former owner.

Can a lien be reduced before you sell?

Sometimes. The city runs a Lien Reduction Program for owners who have done significant work to fix violations, with firm limits.

  • Abatement must be finished before the application, and photos must be dated and time stamped.
  • Liens that were adjudicated or sold at tax sale, liens that were foreclosed on, and paid liens cannot be reduced.
  • Demolition and grass liens can only have interest reduced.
  • Reductions are made per violation, there is no entitlement to one, and there are no appeals. The goal is a response within 30 days.
  • If you pay the lien before the application is processed, the application is denied and the payment is not refunded.

That last rule matters on a closing timeline. Ask the department about a lien payoff and about reduction before any payoff is wired. Forms go to 1340 Poydras Street, Suite 1100, or by email with photos attached, under 25 MB per message.

Short term rental history

A past as a short term rental can change how a house sells. Short term rentals are not legal in New Orleans without a permit, and the rules sit in both the municipal code and the Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance. New regulations passed on March 23, 2023 took effect July 1, 2023.

Short term rental licenses are not transferable, so a buyer cannot simply take over your permit. The application for a residential short term rental owner permit also asks the owner to certify that the dwelling has no outstanding property taxes or city liens on the lot of record.

If you ran an unpermitted rental, the city can send the case to an administrative adjudication hearing, where a hearing officer may impose fines or revoke permits. Clear that history up with the city before you put a closing date on the calendar.

Property tax bills at a sale

The Orleans Parish Assessor sets the assessment and approves exemptions such as the homestead exemption, then certifies the roll to the city Treasurer, who sends the bills. For questions about a valuation, call the assessor at (504) 754-8811.

Bills have gone out online and by mail in January, with payment due by the end of February. Call the Treasury for the current schedule. Assessment appeals go to the Board of Review, which has met at Delgado Community College's City Park campus in the fall, and the City Council's appeals page lists the dates each year.

Closing agents normally prorate the current year's bill between buyer and seller. If the bill is unpaid, ask for a payoff or tax certificate early.

When a cash sale makes sense

A cash sale fits best when the trouble is the house or the calendar. Common examples here are a vacant inherited house with a code case, a property with a lien the owner cannot finance away, a storm-damaged building a lender will not appraise, or a rental that lost its permit.

A cash buyer purchases the property as it stands, so there is no appraisal contingency, no lender repair demands and no showings. You still need clear title, so the lien, tax and recording points above apply to every route. Compare any cash offer against what a listing would net, and ask what each route leaves you after liens and the documentary tax.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to fix code violations before selling a house in New Orleans?

Not always, but open violations can lead to a hearing and a lien, and a lien must be paid or released at closing. Fixing the cited items before a hearing can end the case without further city action.

Who pays the documentary transaction tax on a New Orleans sale?

The seller is one of the parties responsible. The tax is a flat $325 for most documents, paid when the act is recorded.

Where do I record a deed or act of sale in New Orleans?

At the Land Records Division of the Orleans Parish Clerk of Civil District Court, 1340 Poydras Street, 4th Floor. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.

Can I sell a New Orleans house that has an unpermitted short term rental history?

Yes, but the city can pursue unpermitted rentals through adjudication, and permits do not transfer to a buyer. Resolve open cases and any unpaid taxes or liens first.

What if a New Orleans house is in an inherited succession?

Title still has to be sorted out before a sale. The code process researches every person with a legal interest in the property, so an unopened succession can slow a hearing or a sale. Talk to a Louisiana attorney or notary about it.

Baton Rouge: city and parish run together

The Louisiana capital shares one consolidated government with East Baton Rouge Parish. Sellers inside the city limits therefore deal with parish offices for permits, blight enforcement and recording.

The city counted 227,470 residents in 2020 across 86.32 square miles of land, and Greater Baton Rouge held 870,569 people that year. That makes the buyer pool much larger than the city itself. Interstates 10, 12 and 110 connect neighborhoods such as Highland Road, the Garden District, Goodwood, Scotlandville, Mid-City and the Perkins Road area, and Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport serves the region.

State offices, LSU, Southern University and the river port keep demand steady. Roofs, drainage and air conditioning age fast in a climate that averages 61.94 inches of rain a year, and buyers price that wear into their offers.

Baton Rouge housing numbers

Under half of occupied homes in the city are lived in by their owners. These 2020 to 2024 numbers describe the city as a whole, so they say little about any one street. Ask a local agent or appraiser for comparable sales close to your address before you decide what price to hope for.

With over half of homes rented, plenty of local sellers are landlords. A tenant in place, a lease running beyond closing or a unit emptied by a rough move-out changes the options compared with selling your own residence.

How did the August 2016 flood change selling in Baton Rouge?

The August 2016 flood still comes up in nearly every conversation with buyers and lenders. Twenty to 30 inches of rain fell over several days, and rescues topped 30,000, while over 50,000 homes across southern Louisiana were damaged or destroyed. Roughly 109,000 Louisiana homes took water, 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes. Residential damage was estimated at $3.8 billion, with $2.3 billion of it in those two parishes.

Expect questions like these if your house took water:

  • Did the house flood in 2016, and what repairs were permitted?
  • Is there a flood zone determination or elevation record on file?
  • Can you show invoices for post-2016 work?

A buyer who pulls permit history may find unpermitted repairs from that period, and flood zone details can change whether a lender will close. For 2026 the state commission publishes a mandatory Property Disclosure form, so read it early and answer water history questions carefully.

The Comite River Diversion, a 12-mile channel built to cut headwater flooding, is not finished. All 23 contracts had been awarded by the close of fiscal year 2025, and six are under construction. Do not count on lower risk for a given street yet.

Blight and code enforcement

Weeds and brush that reach eight inches count as a nuisance under the city-parish code. A property with a blight violation gets a notice giving the owner 15 days to fix it, plus a blight court date.

Should the problem remain by the hearing, the court may enter a judgment for a fine and costs. The Department of Development may then clear the property and place a lien for the cost. Such a lien sticks to the land, so it gets paid at closing.

  • Report a problem property at 311.
  • Questions about a notice go to Neighborhood Improvement at 225-389-8680.
  • The Department of Development handles construction permits and code enforcement for the parish at 225-389-3171.

Heirs and owners of empty houses often find a blight case only when a lien appears in the title search, so call before you list. The city also has a page on adjudicated property, useful if an inherited house has a history of unpaid taxes.

How a sale closes in East Baton Rouge Parish

Under the Civil Code, selling real estate or promising to sell it takes an authentic act or an act under private signature. The authentic version is signed with a notary and two witnesses, which explains why closings here run through a notary.

After signing, the act of sale is filed with the Clerk of Court for East Baton Rouge Parish. Its Recording Department indexes conveyances by vendee and vendor and collects fees at filing. The number is (225) 389-3985, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 1991, Baton Rouge, LA 70821-1991.

New mandatory forms for 2026, among them the Property Disclosure and the Residential Agreement to Buy or Sell, became effective January 1, 2026. Your closing professional can tell you which ones your sale needs.

Ways to sell a Baton Rouge house

Three routes are common: list the house, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from an investor. Condition, flood history and your timeline decide which one fits.

  • Listing with an agent: Fits a clean, repaired house if you can sit through showings, financing and an appraisal.
  • For sale by owner: Disclosures, buyer screening and notary scheduling become your job.
  • Cash sale as-is: Makes sense for flood damage, postponed repairs, a tenant or a blight notice, since no lender's inspection stands in the way.

Whoever you sell to, read every page of the contract, including any cancellation language, before you sign.

Checklist before you accept an offer

Look at the address first: flood history, code cases, permits and liens. Any of them can move the price or stop a lender.

  • Pull your flood zone and any 2016 water history.
  • Ask 311 or Neighborhood Improvement whether a blight case is open.
  • Order a title search of the conveyance and mortgage records.
  • If you inherited the house, settle who may sign.
  • Keep copies of repair invoices and permits from post-2016 work.

An hour on these steps often saves weeks. Landlords should also dig out the lease and note its end date, because a tenant affects showings and the date keys can change hands.

What to expect on closing day

Closing is a signing appointment at a notary or title office. Bring a photo ID. The notary has the act of sale, payoff figures and settlement statement ready. Taxes, a mortgage balance and recording fees are taken from your proceeds, and the signed act then goes to the clerk. Request the statement early so you can question any fee.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a notary to sell a house in Baton Rouge?

Almost always. Louisiana sales of real estate are made by authentic act or act under private signature, and in practice you sign with a notary. A title company or closing attorney normally sets this up.

Does a Baton Rouge house that flooded in 2016 have to be disclosed?

Buyers and insurers will probably ask, and a mandatory 2026 Property Disclosure form exists. Check with your closing professional how it applies, answer plainly and save repair records.

What happens if my Baton Rouge house has a blight violation?

The owner gets a notice with 15 days to correct the problem and a blight court date. If it is not cleared, the court can assess a fine and costs, and the city can clear the property and place a lien. Call 311 or 225-389-8680 to ask about status.

Where are Baton Rouge deeds recorded?

The Recording Department of the parish Clerk of Court handles it, at (225) 389-3985. You pay fees when the document is filed.

How many Baton Rouge homes are owner-occupied?

Roughly 47.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $234,700. Both are citywide numbers, so a specific house may differ.

Shreveport at a glance

Shreveport is the parish seat of Caddo Parish in northwest Louisiana, on the west bank of the Red River, and part of the city reaches into Bossier Parish. The 2020 census counted 187,593 residents in the city and 393,406 in the Shreveport-Bossier City metro area.

Oil built much of the twentieth century city, and drilling returned later through the Haynesville Shale. Government, health care and education are the biggest employers today, with Barksdale Air Force Base, Caddo Parish Public Schools and Willis-Knighton Medical Center at the top. Many households here depend on the base, the schools or the hospitals, so buyer demand tends to follow those job centers.

Roofs and storm damage

Shreveport has a humid subtropical climate, and spring and summer bring severe thunderstorms with hail, damaging wind and tornadoes. Roofs, gutters and tree limbs take the beating.

An older roof with hail marks or patched leaks gets flagged by a conventional buyer's inspector and insurer, and a repair estimate can move a deal. A cash buyer looks at the same roof but prices the work into the offer, so the repair does not hold up the closing.

Neglected property and city abatement

The city's Department of Property Standards handles abatement of vacant, overgrown and unsafe property. A legal notice the city published in October 2025 shows how the process works and what an owner faces.

  • Owners listed in a notice like that one must fix care of premises, securing and inoperable vehicle violations within 10 days of publication, and demolitions within 30 days.
  • If an owner does not comply, the city can do the work with its own crews or a contractor, and the cost is the owner's responsibility.
  • The city adds an administrative charge of $500 on top of the work, and it may enforce a lien under its ordinance and state law.
  • Environmental Court fines run up to $75 per day per violation on residential property and $300 on commercial property, with a $5,000 cap for residential fines. Owners age 65 and older get an additional 30 days before enforcement.
  • A written appeal is due within 10 days of publication, sent to the Department of Property Standards at P. O. Box 31109, Shreveport, LA 71130.

Anyone acquiring an interest in a listed property is subject to its requirements, so a buyer inherits the problem along with the house. Many of the addresses in such notices are held by estates or unopened successions, which is where a lot of heirs here find themselves.

How Shreveport and Caddo Parish bill property tax

Two bills may apply: one for the parish and one for the city's downtown district if the property sits in it. The Caddo Parish Assessor values the property, and you can reach that office at 318-226-6701. Notices for the city and the Downtown Development Authority (Central Business District) go out in mid-November, with payment due December 31 to the City Finance Department.

The Caddo Parish Sheriff collects parish taxes, also due by December 31. Mailed payments go to PO Box 20905, Shreveport, LA 71120-0905. At closing the title company prorates the year's bill, so ask early whether the current bill has been paid.

What recording a sale costs in Caddo Parish

The Caddo Parish Clerk records deeds, mortgages, rights of way, powers of attorney, judgments and tax liens. Conveyance and mortgage fees run by page count.

An additional $5 fee for the statewide records authority starts January 1, 2027. The record room can help you locate a document but cannot do a title search. Conveyances are indexed back to 1914 and scanned back to 1838.

Selling an inherited house

Heirs make up a large share of the owners who end up with a city notice. A house left behind after a death often sits empty while the family sorts out who owns it, and grass grows and windows go unsecured in the meantime. The city's clock does not wait for the succession.

If that is your situation, gather the death records and any will you have, and see a Louisiana attorney or notary about the succession. Tell any buyer up front that an estate is involved. A buyer who knows early can plan the closing date around the court steps, and a cash buyer will usually take the house with the notices and the grass included in the price.

Keep the tax side moving too. The Sheriff's office and the City Finance Department will each tell you what is owed on the address, and a title company will want both figures before it schedules the act of sale.

When a cash sale makes sense in Shreveport

The situations that tend to fit are an inherited house with open Property Standards notices, a vacant property with grass or securing violations, a house with roof or storm damage, or a rental with long-term tenant problems. In each case the owner wants a firm closing date and a buyer who will take the property as it is.

Title still has to be clear. Sort out any lien from a city abatement, any unpaid tax and any succession questions with a Louisiana notary or attorney before the act of sale. Compare a cash price with what a listing would net after repairs, carrying costs and commissions.

Steps to sell a house that has city notices or back taxes

Start with the paperwork, since most delays here trace back to it. These steps work for a conventional sale and a cash sale alike.

  1. Look up any open Property Standards notice on the address and note the deadlines on it.
  2. Ask the city for the cost of any abatement work it has already done, since that amount can become a lien.
  3. Ask the Sheriff's office and the City Finance Department whether this year's bill has been paid.
  4. Order a mortgage certificate from the clerk, at the fee in the table above, to see what is recorded against the house.
  5. If an owner has died, talk to a Louisiana attorney or notary about whether a judgment of possession is needed before an act of sale can be signed.
  6. Pick the route, listing or cash, and compare what each leaves you after liens, taxes and recording.

A buyer paying cash can skip the appraisal and the lender's repair list, but the title work in steps three and four still happens.

How long do I have to fix a Shreveport property standards violation?

In the city's October 2025 notice, owners had 10 days from publication for care of premises, securing and vehicle violations and 30 days for demolitions. Appeals were due within 10 days.

Can the City of Shreveport put a lien on my house?

Yes. If the city has to do the abatement work, the owner owes the cost plus a $500 administrative charge, and the city can enforce a lien under its ordinance and state law.

When are Caddo Parish property taxes due?

They are due by December 31 of the year assessed. City and downtown district notices are mailed in mid-November.

What does it cost to record a deed in Caddo Parish?

A conveyance of 1 to 5 pages is $105, 6 to 25 pages is $205, and 26 to 50 pages is $305. Fees can change, so confirm with the clerk.

Can heirs sell a Shreveport house before the succession is finished?

Lafayette in context

Acadiana's biggest hub, Lafayette, is where Lafayette Parish keeps its government, along the Vermilion River. In 2020 the city held 121,374 people, the consolidated city-parish 241,753 (up from 221,578 in 2010) and the metro area 478,384. New Orleans is 135 miles away, Baton Rouge 59 and Lake Charles 75. Broussard, Carencro, Scott, Youngsville and Duson are smaller municipalities inside the parish.

Energy, health care, education, technology and retail all employ local buyers. The University of Louisiana at Lafayette enrolls over 18,000 students. Oil and gas work moves with crude prices, which can push a household into a quick sale. Interstates 10 and 49 and U.S. highways 90 and 167 make commuting simple. Homes close to downtown can be quite old, and age brings repair lists.

Is flooding a concern for a Lafayette house?

The city rests on higher ground than much of south Louisiana, so serious flooding is mostly local flash flooding. Still, no lot is automatically safe. Development spans both banks of the Vermilion, and several coulees, Isaac Verot Coulee and Coulee des Poches among them, drain into it. Insurers and buyers check flood zones, so find your address on the map before listing and write down any past water.

Rain falls all year, most heavily in summer. Heat and moisture wear out cooling systems, roofs and attic vents, and a hard freeze can crack pipes. The age of the air conditioner and roof will come up with buyers.

Property taxes and homestead

The Lafayette Parish Assessor sets values, while bodies like the city-parish and the school board set rates. Every property must be reassessed at least once in four years, and values can still move yearly with sales.

Homestead protects the first $7,500 of assessed value (worth $75,000 of market value) on the owner's residence. A pool, outdoor kitchen, pool house or storage building owned by the same person is included. A second house or commercial building on the lot is not.

How do I appeal a Lafayette assessment, and when is tax due?

Begin with a deputy assessor and show evidence that the value exceeds the market. Unresolved? Next comes the Lafayette Consolidated Council, which hears appeals in September, then the Louisiana Tax Commission, then district court within thirty days.
